strengths: The paper proposes a simple, training-free adaptation of ReID features for MOT: using historical trajectory features to compute an FLD/LDA-style per-sequence projection, with temporal centroid weighting and fusion with the original feature space. The idea is intuitive and well matched to MOT settings where identities in a sequence occupy a narrow and locally confusing part of the global ReID space.

The empirical gains over the authors' feature-only baseline are large, especially on DanceTrack and SportsMOT, and the ablations support the main design choices: FLD is substantially better than PCA, temporal weighting helps, and mixing projected/original similarities improves robustness.

The evaluation covers several relevant regimes, including DanceTrack, MOT17, SportsMOT, TAO, and zero-shot MASA features. The zero-shot experiments are a useful addition because they suggest the method is not tied to one ReID backbone.

The method is practically attractive: it is modular, does not require retraining, and can be applied on top of existing extracted features. The paper also includes useful discussion of inference speed and limitations.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. FLD/LDA is a classical discriminative projection, and the main contribution is its online application to trajectory-conditioned ReID features plus reasonable MOT-specific modifications. This is elegant, but not deeply novel algorithmically.

The strongest results are shown for a custom feature-only tracker. The paper argues that appearance can be much stronger than commonly assumed, but it does not convincingly demonstrate how much the proposed transformation improves established hybrid trackers such as Deep OC-SORT, BoT-SORT, or DiffMOT when inserted into their association pipelines.

Comparison fairness is somewhat difficult to judge. Detectors, validation/test usage, hyperparameter tuning, and daggered results are not always fully disentangled. The paper states that some hyperparameters are adjusted across datasets, while ablations tune settings on validation data; this weakens the claim of a universally robust training-free module.

The method depends on track histories produced by the tracker itself, so ID switches or early assignment errors can contaminate the class labels used by FLD. The paper acknowledges this risk but does not provide a targeted stress test, failure analysis, or quantitative robustness evaluation under noisy histories/occlusions/crowded scenes.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the abstract says code will be released but the link is empty, and several implementation details needed to reproduce benchmark submissions are deferred or summarized at a high level.

There are clarity and technical-presentation issues. For example, the FLD class mean equation appears to use 1/N rather than 1/N_c, terminology alternates between FLD/LDA/Trans-FastReID/HAT-FastReID, and some tables contain duplicated or confusing entries. These issues do not invalidate the idea but make the scientific case less crisp.

The computational cost is nontrivial: 22.7 FPS is reported given detections, with generalized eigenvalue computation on CPU as the bottleneck. The scaling with feature dimension, number of active identities, and frame density is not analyzed enough for deployment-heavy MOT settings.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and relevant issue in MOT: generic ReID embeddings are often used naively, while association only needs to discriminate identities within the current sequence. This is a sensible framing for an Algorithms/General contribution.

The proposed method is simple and training-free: using historical trajectory features to construct an FLD/LDA-style projection, temporal weighting, and fusion with the original cosine similarity. This makes the idea easy to integrate into conventional tracking-by-detection pipelines.

The reported gains over the authors' ReID-only baseline are large on DanceTrack and SportsMOT, especially in AssA/IDF1, and the zero-shot MASA experiments suggest the transformation can help multiple feature extractors rather than only one trained ReID model.

The ablations cover the main components: FLD versus PCA, history length, temporal weighting, and original/transformed feature fusion. These experiments support the claim that the improvement is not solely from one tuned hyperparameter.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The core method is essentially online LDA/FLD applied to pseudo-labeled track histories, plus exponential temporal weighting and score fusion. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish this from classic adaptive metric learning, discriminant subspace learning, or prior MOT methods that update appearance models online.

There are technical soundness gaps in the FLD formulation and implementation. Eq. 6 appears to divide the class mean by N rather than Nc; the paper does not explain regularization or numerical handling when Sw is singular, when few samples/classes exist, or when the number of active trajectories changes rapidly. These are central issues for online LDA in tracking, not minor details.

The approach relies on previous tracker assignments as labels, but the paper gives little analysis of error amplification under ID switches, occlusion, fragmented tracks, or newborn identities. A method that maximizes separation based on potentially wrong pseudo-labels needs robustness analysis beyond aggregate benchmark scores.

The experimental comparison is not fully convincing. The headline claim that a feature-only tracker matches or surpasses state of the art is weakened by unclear detector/control settings, duplicated or inconsistently presented SportsMOT rows, and comparisons to methods that may use different detections, training data, or validation/test protocols.

Hyperparameter tuning raises reproducibility and fairness concerns. The appendix says grid search is performed on the corresponding datasets, and the daggered results adjust hyperparameters across datasets, but it is not clear whether validation-only tuning was used for all reported test numbers. This ambiguity is serious for benchmark claims.

The paper omits important baselines that would isolate the actual contribution, such as regularized LDA variants, nearest-class-centroid updates, online metric learning, whitening/Mahalanobis distance, simple per-sequence feature normalization, and stronger appearance-only tracking baselines.

The method introduces notable computational overhead from repeated generalized eigenvalue decompositions, yet runtime is only briefly discussed in the appendix. The reported 22.7 FPS given detections may be acceptable, but the scalability with number of tracks, feature dimension, and crowded scenes is not adequately characterized.

Several claims are overstated. The paper says the method 'clearly demonstrates' the superiority/potential of appearance features and suggests reconsidering tracker design, but the method intentionally excludes motion cues and does not show integration with strong hybrid trackers or consistent improvements over the best full systems.

Clarity and polish are uneven. There are typos and awkward notation, missing code link content in the abstract, inconsistent names such as HAT-FastReID-MOT versus Trans-FastReID-MOT, and some visualization/table labels are hard to parse. These issues do not alone determine rejection, but they compound reproducibility concerns.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, well-motivated idea: adapt generic ReID embeddings at inference time for each video sequence using history-aware Fisher Linear Discriminant projection, with temporal centroid weighting and fusion with the original feature space. The framing that MOT requires sequence-specific discrimination rather than globally generic ReID separation is compelling and relevant.

The method is training-free, modular, and easy to integrate into existing tracking-by-detection pipelines. This gives the contribution practical appeal, especially because it improves appearance-only tracking without requiring new labeled training data.

Experimental evidence is broad and generally convincing. The method improves a naive FastReID-based tracker substantially on DanceTrack and SportsMOT, remains competitive on MOT17, and gives consistent zero-shot gains when applied to MASA features across DanceTrack, SportsMOT, and TAO.

The ablations are useful and targeted: the paper compares FLD against PCA, studies history length, temporal weighting, and the fusion coefficient, and shows that most gains come from the proposed history-conditioned discriminative projection rather than from incidental parameter changes.

The manuscript is mostly clear and logically organized, with helpful visualizations and an explicit limitations section. The discussion of why appearance cues have been underused in MOT is thoughtful and could stimulate useful follow-up work.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental from an algorithmic standpoint: applying FLD/LDA-style projection to online ReID histories is elegant, but the core mathematical tool is classical. The main contribution is the MOT-specific adaptation and empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new learning method.

Some implementation details are underspecified for reproducibility. In particular, the paper should clarify numerical stabilization/regularization for the generalized eigenproblem, handling of singular within-class scatter matrices, behavior when few trajectories or short histories are available, and exact update/recompute schedule.

The comparison protocol raises some fairness questions. Several results use dataset-specific tuned hyperparameters marked with a dagger, while the boundary between validation tuning and test reporting is not always fully clear. SportsMOT Table 3 includes duplicated method names and gray joint-training entries that make interpretation harder.

The method depends on previous tracking assignments as pseudo-labels for FLD. The paper acknowledges sensitivity to ID misallocation but does not deeply analyze failure cases, error accumulation, crowded identity-switch scenarios, or robustness under poor detections and severe occlusion.

Runtime is acceptable but not negligible: the appendix reports 22.7 FPS given detections and attributes most added latency to CPU eigen-decomposition. For high-density scenes or lower-resource deployment, the computational scaling with number of active tracks and feature dimension should be characterized more thoroughly.

The code-release statement appears incomplete in the abstract, and reproducibility would benefit from released configs, fixed detector outputs, and exact hyperparameter grids. Without these, some of the large reported gains may be harder to independently verify.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and relevant mismatch in MOT practice: generic open-set ReID embeddings are used unchanged for a sequence-specific association problem. The proposed history-aware FLD/LDA transformation is simple, training-free, and well motivated by the discriminability analysis linking the proposed δ1000 measure to AssA.

The empirical gains are substantial on the settings where the method is most targeted. FastReID-MOT improves from 50.6 to 58.6/61.2 HOTA on DanceTrack and from 67.3 to 78.1/78.9 HOTA on SportsMOT, with especially large AssA gains. The method also improves hybrid trackers and MASA variants across DanceTrack, SportsMOT, and TAO, suggesting the idea is not tied to one backbone.

The ablation study is relatively thorough. The paper compares FLD against PCA, studies oracle versus YOLOX detections, tests history length, temporal decay, and fusion coefficient, and includes a useful supervised-FLD comparison showing that sequence-local history matters more than a globally fitted projection.

The paper is clear about several limitations: gains are smaller on MOT17 and TAO where appearance ambiguity is lower, gains in hybrid trackers are limited by motion-first designs, and the method does not directly apply to end-to-end trackers. Reporting inference speed and identifying generalized eigenvalue computation as the main bottleneck improves transparency.

The presentation is generally readable and the method is easy to reproduce conceptually: use recent track histories as pseudo-labels/classes, compute an FLD projection online, and fuse similarities from the transformed and original spaces.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is moderate. Applying classical FLD/LDA to recent track histories is elegant and effective, but the method is largely a well-known supervised projection technique adapted to MOT rather than a deeply new algorithmic formulation.

The strongest results are concentrated on appearance-ambiguous benchmarks and ReID-heavy baselines. On MOT17, the gain for the hybrid tracker is almost negligible (64.1 to 64.2 HOTA), and on TAO the improvements are small. This narrows the practical impact relative to the broad claims that MOT generally favors context-specific representation.

The comparisons against recent systems are somewhat selective. The paper acknowledges not including some recent hybrid trackers due to tuning complexity and cue dilution, but this weakens the state-of-the-art claims, especially for a conference-level empirical paper.

The method adds a notable runtime cost: 22.7 FPS versus 46.5 FPS for the baseline excluding detector latency. This is still usable, but the cost is significant for an online tracking component and the proposed speedups are speculative rather than demonstrated.

There are technical details that need sharper specification for reproducibility and robustness, such as numerical regularization of the within-class scatter matrix, behavior when the number of active trajectories is small, handling noisy early track histories, and exact update/recompute frequency. These issues matter because the method depends on online pseudo-labels that may contain tracking errors.

The manuscript occasionally overstates its conclusions, for example framing direct ReID use as fundamentally inappropriate and claiming new state-of-the-art performance, while the evidence supports a more nuanced claim: sequence-adaptive appearance projection is highly beneficial in visually ambiguous, ReID-relevant regimes but less decisive elsewhere.

strengths: The paper identifies a reasonable mismatch between generic ReID embeddings and the sequence-specific discrimination needed in MOT, and the proposed use of history-conditioned FLD/LDA is simple, interpretable, and training-free.

The experimental section is broad in scope: DanceTrack, SportsMOT, TAO, MOT17, MOT20 validation, multiple ReID backbones via MASA, and insertion into several hybrid trackers. The reported gains on association metrics are often large, especially on DanceTrack and SportsMOT.

The ablations are useful and mostly aligned with the method: transformation choice, history length, temporal weighting, similarity fusion, and comparison to a supervised FLD variant all help isolate why the method may work.
The paper discusses limitations such as weaker gains for hybrid trackers, limited applicability to end-to-end trackers, and nontrivial runtime overhead from generalized eigenvalue computation.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is essentially applying classical FLD/LDA online to predicted track histories, plus a weighted centroid and score fusion. This is elegant but not very original algorithmically, and the paper overstates the conceptual novelty with claims such as the direct ReID practice being 'fundamentally inappropriate'.

The evaluation protocol raises concerns. The paper states that hyperparameters are exhaustively grid-searched per benchmark and that daggered results are tuned on the corresponding dataset to maximize performance, but it is not sufficiently clear what data split is used for tuning versus test reporting. This is especially problematic for SOTA claims on benchmark test sets.

The strongest results rely on a self-constructed FastReID-MOT baseline and modified tracker variants such as ByteTrack-ReID, OC-SORT-ReID, and HAT-Hybrid-SORT-ReID. Implementation details for these integrations and fusion choices are not enough to make the comparisons fully reproducible or to rule out confounding from tracker engineering.

The method can self-reinforce tracking errors because the FLD labels are previous tracker assignments. The paper acknowledges possible history errors but does not provide a convincing stress test under identity switches, occlusion-heavy cases, early-track instability, or noisy detections beyond aggregate benchmark results.

The claimed state-of-the-art case is selective. The paper admits that several recent trackers are omitted, and the comparison mixes ReID-only, motion-based, hybrid, and end-to-end methods with different detectors, training data, and tuning practices. This weakens the force of the performance claims.

Runtime is a real drawback: the reported speed drops from 46.5 FPS to 22.7 FPS excluding detector latency. The appendix frames this mainly as an engineering issue, but for online MOT this is a substantive limitation, particularly in crowded scenes where trajectory count increases.

The analysis metric δ1000 is plausible but somewhat hand-designed, and the correlation analysis does not establish causality. Since the method optimizes a related notion of separation, stronger validation would require more direct failure-mode analysis and statistical reporting across sequences.

Presentation is generally understandable, but several claims are rhetorically inflated relative to the modest algorithmic advance, and some equations/text extraction in the manuscript appear poorly formatted, which hurts clarity.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and underexplored mismatch between generic ReID embeddings and the sequence-specific discrimination required for MOT. The proposed history-aware FLD transformation is simple, training-free, and conceptually well matched to the problem.

The empirical evidence is strong for an Algorithms/General contribution: large gains over a carefully tuned FastReID-MOT baseline on DanceTrack and SportsMOT, consistent improvements when integrated into ByteTrack/OC-SORT/Hybrid-SORT variants, and broad improvements across MASA backbones and TAO.

The ablation study is convincing. The paper separately evaluates FLD vs PCA, history-aware fitting vs supervised cross-video FLD, history length, temporal weighting, and score-level knowledge integration, which supports the main design choices rather than only reporting end metrics.

The work is practically attractive because it can be plugged into existing tracking-by-detection systems without retraining. The authors also report inference speed and discuss the main computational bottleneck, which helps assess deployment tradeoffs.

The limitations are unusually clear: gains are smaller on hybrid trackers, MOT17/TAO have less headroom due to stronger inherent visual separability, and the method is not directly applicable to current end-to-end query-based trackers.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is moderate: the method adapts classical FLD/LDA using track histories, with useful MOT-specific engineering, but it is not a fundamentally new learning or optimization framework.

The strongest claims are concentrated on benchmarks where appearance ambiguity is high and the method is naturally advantaged. Results on MOT17, TAO, and some hybrid settings are positive but modest, suggesting the impact may be scenario-dependent rather than universally transformative.

The comparison to recent trackers is somewhat selective. The appendix acknowledges that newer heuristic methods and heavily tuned systems are not fully explored, which weakens the state-of-the-art claim even though the main experimental case remains persuasive.

The method depends on historical track assignments being sufficiently reliable. The paper discusses this and mitigates it through similarity fusion, but a deeper failure analysis under early identity errors, long occlusions, or dense scenes would make the robustness case stronger.

The inference overhead is substantial: the reported speed drops from 46.5 FPS to 22.7 FPS excluding detection, mainly due to generalized eigen decomposition. This is acceptable for many uses but limits the appeal of the method as a lightweight plug-in until better implementation support is demonstrated.
